books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, C. Workers and New Methods of Production
The North and the Textile Industry

stimulus.text: A magazine cover from August 1845. The title “LOWELL OFFERING” arches over a scene of a young woman in a long dress holding a book, with mill buildings behind her and a beehive at the left. Below the scene, the cover reads: “A REPOSITORY OF ORIGINAL ARTICLES, WRITTEN BY “FACTORY GIRLS.”” The publisher’s line reads “LOWELL: MISS CURTIS & FARLEY. 1845.”
stimulus.source_note: Cover of the Lowell Offering, August 1845, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Image viewed before writing; cover text transcribed from the image.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The cover's description of the magazine as a repository of original articles written by “factory girls” best shows that the Lowell mills

options.text: hired only women who had already published books
options.misconception: The cover says the articles were written by factory girls, not by women who were authors before they were hired.

options.text: kept their workers from reading or writing
options.misconception: The cover itself is a magazine written by the workers, so the mills did not keep them from writing.

options.text: paid women the same wages as men
options.misconception: The cover says nothing about wages, and the mills paid women less than men, which was part of why they were hired.

options.text: presented their workers as respectable, educated young women

rationales.A: The writers were mill workers who wrote while employed, not published authors hired for their books. The cover celebrates workers who wrote, not authors who became workers.
rationales.B: A magazine written by the workers proves the opposite. The mills encouraged reading and writing, and the workers even ran circulating libraries.
rationales.C: Nothing on the cover mentions pay. The mills hired young women partly because they could be paid less than men.
rationales.D: The cover shows a well-dressed young woman holding a book, with mills behind her, and calls the writers factory girls. The image sells the mills as respectable places where educated farm daughters worked for a time.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the picture, not just the words. A well-dressed young woman holds a book, with mills behind her.
2. Read the cover line. It calls the writers factory girls and prints their original articles.
3. Put the two together. The mills are presenting their workers as educated and respectable.
Background: Mill owners recruited farm daughters by promising supervised boardinghouses, cash wages, and cultural events.
Remember: a cover is an argument, so ask what picture of its subject the publisher wants you to see.

figures.caption: Cover of the Lowell Offering, August 1845, a magazine written by mill workers.
